claim: Genome sequences diverge more rapidly in mammals than in other animal lineages, such as birds or insects.
source: Genome sequences diverge more rapidly in mammals than in other animal lineages, such as birds or insects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact and is supported by citations in the introduction (Siepel et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: Recent reports have indicated a faster divergence of transcription factor binding in mammals than in insects.
source: Recent reports have indicated a faster divergence of transcription factor binding in mammals than in insects, but others found the reverse for mRNA expression.
evidence: This claim references previous studies and is supported by citations (Villar et al., 2014; Stefflova et al., 2013).

claim: Some studies found the reverse pattern for mRNA expression, with slower divergence in mammals than in flies.
source: Recent reports have indicated a faster divergence of transcription factor binding in mammals than in insects, but others found the reverse for mRNA expression.
evidence: This claim references previous conflicting findings and is supported by citation (Coolon et al., 2014).

claim: Conflicting interpretations about transcriptional evolution rates resulted from differing methodologies.
source: Here, we show that these conflicting interpretations resulted from differing methodologies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the systematic analysis of different analytical methods shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transcriptional networks evolve at a common rate across mammals, birds and insects.
source: Strikingly, we found that transcriptional networks evolve at a common rate across the three animal lineages.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by data from Figures 3, 4, and 5 showing similar evolutionary rates across lineages.

claim: Differences in rates of genome divergence were greatly reduced when restricting comparisons to chromatin-accessible sequences.
source: Furthermore, differences in rates of genome divergence were greatly reduced when restricting comparisons to chromatin-accessible sequences.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5c,d comparing accessible and inaccessible chromatin regions.

claim: The evolution of transcription is decoupled from the global rate of genome sequence evolution.
source: The evolution of transcription is thus decoupled from the global rate of genome sequence evolution, suggesting that a small fraction of the genome regulates transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that transcriptional networks evolve at similar rates despite different genome-wide divergence rates.

claim: A small fraction of the genome regulates transcription.
source: The evolution of transcription is thus decoupled from the global rate of genome sequence evolution, suggesting that a small fraction of the genome regulates transcription.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the findings, supported by the observation that chromatin-accessible regions show different evolutionary patterns than the genome as a whole.

claim: Recent studies of chromatin structure have implicated half of the human genome in regulatory interactions.
source: Recent studies of chromatin structure have implicated half of the human genome in regulatory interactions (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the ENCODE Project.

claim: Less than 10% of the human genome is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Comparative genomic studies, however, have shown that less than 10% of the human genome is evolutionarily conserved (Siepel et al., 2005), suggesting that many of the experimentally-detected interactions are not functional (Graur et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to comparative genomic studies.

claim: Many experimentally-detected regulatory interactions may not be functional.
source: Comparative genomic studies, however, have shown that less than 10% of the human genome is evolutionarily conserved (Siepel et al., 2005), suggesting that many of the experimentally-detected interactions are not functional (Graur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation suggested by the discrepancy between experimental and evolutionary data, supported by citation.

claim: Genomic sequences can influence transcription even in the absence of evolutionary conservation.
source: These experiments demonstrated that genomic sequences can influence transcription even in the absence of evolutionary conservation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Cookson et al., 2009; McVicker et al., 2013; Kasowski et al., 2010; 2013; Heinz et al., 2013; Villar et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2015; Brem et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2009; Shibata et al., 2012).

claim: Some repetitive elements previously thought to be 'junk' DNA have been shown to effectively regulate gene expression.
source: For instance, some repetitive elements previously thought to be 'junk' DNA have been shown to effectively regulate gene expression (Rebollo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Mammalian genomes contain far more repetitive elements than bird or insect genomes.
source: Such rapid transcriptional evolution would set mammals apart from other metazoans like birds or insects, whose genomes contain far fewer repetitive elements (Taft et al., 2007) and tend to be more constrained (Siepel et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Bird and insect genomes tend to be more constrained than mammalian genomes.
source: Such rapid transcriptional evolution would set mammals apart from other metazoans like birds or insects, whose genomes contain far fewer repetitive elements (Taft et al., 2007) and tend to be more constrained (Siepel et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: ChIP studies in mammalian livers have generally described faster divergence rates than similar studies in fly embryos.
source: When examining the evolution of GSTF binding, chromatin immuno-precipitation (ChIP) studies in mammalian livers have generally described faster divergence rates than similar studies in fly embryos (Villar et al., 2014; Stefflova et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Divergence rates in previous ChIP studies were estimated with different analytical methods.
source: However, divergence rates were estimated with different analytical methods in the different ChIP studies (Supplementary file 1) (Villar et al., 2014; Bardet et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 1 and citations.

claim: Gene expression levels may diverge at a slower rate in mammals than in flies.
source: Another study found that gene expression levels may diverge at a slower rate in mammals than in flies, by comparing genome-wide correlations of mRNA abundances estimated by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) for mammals but by a mixture of technologies for flies including microarrays (Coolon et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The study assembled a comparative genomics platform encompassing >40 publicly available datasets spanning >25 organisms representative of Mammalia, Aves and Insecta.
source: We assembled a comparative genomics platform encompassing >40 publicly available datasets spanning >25 organisms representative of the Mammalia (mammals), Aves (birds) and Insecta (insects) phylogenetic classes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study design, supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The statistical framework could detect differences in divergence rates with high sensitivity.
source: We assessed the power of this statistical framework using simulations and found that it could detect differences in divergence rates with high sensitivity (Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genomic segments retaining homologs displayed high sequence conservation across all three lineages.
source: Segments retaining homologs displayed high sequence conservation across all three lineages, although our framework detected a slightly but significantly faster divergence in insects than in mammals or birds (P<0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Insects show slightly but significantly faster nucleotide substitution rates than mammals or birds in conserved segments.
source: Segments retaining homologs displayed high sequence conservation across all three lineages, although our framework detected a slightly but significantly faster divergence in insects than in mammals or birds (P<0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 100 million years of evolution, only ~30% of mammalian segments retained homology, whereas >60% of bird and insect segments did.
source: For instance, after 100 million years (Myrs) of evolution, only ~30% of mammalian segments retained homology, whereas >60% of bird and insect segments did.
evidence: This claim is derived from data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The findings recapitulated previous observations that genome sequences are less constrained in mammals than in insects or birds.
source: These findings recapitulated previous observations according to which genome sequences are less constrained in mammals than in insects (Siepel et al., 2005) or birds (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim connects the study's findings to previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Correlations of gene expression levels decreased over time at similar rates that were statistically indistinguishable across lineages.
source: We found that correlations of gene expression levels decreased over time at similar rates that were statistically indistinguishable: a lineage-naïve model describing the evolution of gene expression levels under a common rate fitted the data as well as a lineage-aware model (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The result that gene expression levels evolve at similar rates was robust to changes in correlation metrics or inclusion/exclusion of poorly expressed genes.
source: This result was robust to changes in correlation metrics or inclusion/exclusion of poorly expressed genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gene expression levels can remain relatively stable even as the genomic locations bound by GSTFs change rapidly over time.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that gene expression levels can remain relatively stable even as the genomic locations bound by GSTFs change rapidly over time (Wong et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2009; Paris et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is no consensus on the appropriate analytical method for ChIP-seq analysis.
source: Despite the widespread use of ChIP-seq, there is no consensus on the appropriate analytical method (Wilbanks and Facciotti, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Analytical choices in ChIP-seq analysis can strongly influence downstream findings.
source: Further comparison of occupied segments across species requires additional analytical choices (Figure 4a), some of which can strongly influence downstream findings (Bardet et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: The study executed 108 analytical pipelines to compare divergence rates across 6 pairs of GSTFs.
source: In total, we executed 108 analytical pipelines to compare divergence rates across 6 pairs of GSTFs (2 in insects each compared with 3 in mammals), the occupancy profiles of which were examined in 3–7 species per lineage (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology.

claim: In the majority of cases (56–78% over the 6 comparisons), GSTF binding patterns diverged at statistically indistinguishable rates in mammals and insects.
source: However, in the majority of cases (56–78% over the 6 comparisons), GSTF binding patterns diverged at statistically indistinguishable rates in mammals and insects (Figure 4d; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: After 100 Myrs of evolution, the correlation of GSTF occupancy profiles was 0.10 in mammals and 0.13 in insects.
source: After 100 Myrs of evolution, the correlation of GSTF occupancy profiles was 0.10 in mammals and 0.13 in insects.
evidence: This claim is derived from the nucleotide-resolution analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Patterns of DNA occupancy are more conserved for CTCF than for GSTFs in mammals.
source: In mammals, patterns of DNA occupancy have been shown to be more conserved for CTCF than for GSTFs using unified analytical methods (Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: CTCF DNA occupancy diverges rapidly in insects, perhaps due to the existence of other insulator proteins.
source: In contrast, CTCF DNA occupancy was shown to diverge rapidly in insects, perhaps due to the existence of other insulator proteins (Villar et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The analysis successfully recapitulated the difference in CTCF conservation between mammals and insects.
source: Our analysis successfully recapitulated this difference (Figure 4f), demonstrating that the common evolutionary rate observed among GSTFs (Figure 4e) was not an artifact of our method for profile correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4f and serves as a validation of the method.

claim: DNA sequence motifs for GSTFs are retained at similar, indistinguishable rates in mammals and insects.
source: We found similar, indistinguishable retention rates in mammals and insects (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Motifs for GSTFs shared between M. musculus and D. melanogaster were retained at similar rates across lineages in 8 out of 12 cases.
source: We found that these motifs were retained at similar rates across lineages relative to background expectations in 8 out of 12 cases (one example shown in Figure 5b; all other cases in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most active cis-regulatory sequences are located in genomic regions with accessible chromatin.
source: Most active cis-regulatory sequences are located in genomic regions with accessible chromatin (Hesselberth et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Chromatin-accessible sequences are significantly more conserved between human and mouse than expected by chance.
source: A recent study showed that chromatin-accessible sequences were significantly more conserved between human and mouse than expected by chance (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Inaccessible segments lost homology much faster in mammals than in insects and birds.
source: Whereas inaccessible segments lost homology much faster in mammals than in insects and birds (P<0.05; Figure 5c), accessible segments retained homologs at more similar rates in the three lineages (Figure 5d; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Accessible segments retained homologs at more similar rates in the three lineages compared to inaccessible segments.
source: Whereas inaccessible segments lost homology much faster in mammals than in insects and birds (P<0.05; Figure 5c), accessible segments retained homologs at more similar rates in the three lineages (Figure 5d; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Approximately 50% of chromatin-accessible segments and only ~20% of inaccessible segments retained homology after 100 Myrs in mammals.
source: For instance, ~60% of segments retained homology after 100 Myrs in birds and insects, independently of accessibility, whereas ~50% of chromatin-accessible segments and only ~20% of inaccessible segments did so in mammals.
evidence: This claim is derived from data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: Approximately 60% of segments retained homology after 100 Myrs in birds and insects, independently of accessibility.
source: For instance, ~60% of segments retained homology after 100 Myrs in birds and insects, independently of accessibility, whereas ~50% of chromatin-accessible segments and only ~20% of inaccessible segments did so in mammals.
evidence: This claim is derived from data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: The analyses represent the most comprehensive study conducted to date on the evolution of transcriptional networks across animal lineages.
source: To our knowledge, the analyses presented here represent the most comprehensive study conducted to date on the evolution of transcriptional networks across animal lineages.
evidence: This is a claim about the scope of the study.

claim: Gene expression levels, GSTF binding patterns, regulatory motifs and chromatin-accessible sequences each diverged at rates that were similar across mammals, birds and insects.
source: We observed that gene expression levels, GSTF binding patterns, regulatory motifs and chromatin-accessible sequences each diverged at rates that were similar across mammals, birds and insects.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings, supported by data from Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The results reconcile previously conflicting findings about transcriptional evolution rates.
source: These unexpected results reconcile previously conflicting findings (Villar et al., 2014; Coolon et al., 2014), highlighting the importance of unified study methodologies and providing evidence for a common evolutionary rate in metazoan transcriptional networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's contribution, supported by citations to previous conflicting studies.

claim: The results highlight the importance of unified study methodologies.
source: These unexpected results reconcile previously conflicting findings (Villar et al., 2014; Coolon et al., 2014), highlighting the importance of unified study methodologies and providing evidence for a common evolutionary rate in metazoan transcriptional networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that different methodologies led to different conclusions in previous studies.

claim: Data on closely related species are needed to investigate the dynamics of molecular network evolution.
source: However, data on closely related species, like those which we collected in this study, are needed to investigate the dynamics of molecular network evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for studying molecular evolution.

claim: The study only investigated three lineages and six to twelve organisms per lineage with non-uniform coverage over evolutionary time.
source: We only investigated three lineages and six to twelve organisms per lineage with non-uniform coverage over evolutionary time.
evidence: This is a description of the study's limitations.

claim: The study only examined a small number of tissues for each lineage and a total of five GSTFs (none in birds).
source: In addition, we only examined a small number of tissues for each lineage and a total of five GSTFs (none in birds).
evidence: This is a description of the study's limitations.

claim: Mammals, birds and insects exhibit wide differences in features traditionally associated with evolutionary rates, such as generation times and breeding sizes.
source: Mammals, birds and insects exhibit wide differences in the features that are traditionally associated with evolutionary rates, such as generation times and breeding sizes.
evidence: This is a statement about known biological differences between lineages.

claim: Populations with small breeding sizes, such as mammals, are thought to be more prone to genetic drift.
source: Populations with small breeding sizes, such as mammals, are thought to be more prone to genetic drift (Ohta, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to population genetics theory.

claim: Genetic drift theory accounts for the abundance of repetitive elements and the rapid evolution of genomic sequences in mammals relative to insects.
source: This theory accounts for the abundance of repetitive elements and the rapid evolution of genomic sequences in mammals relative to insects, which have much larger breeding sizes.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting population genetics theory to observed genomic patterns.

claim: Repetitive and rapidly-evolving sequences make up the majority of the mammalian genome.
source: One potential model could be that repetitive and rapidly-evolving sequences, which make up the majority of the mammalian genome (Siepel et al., 2005; Taft et al., 2007), play a negligible role in the global regulation of gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Chromatin-accessible regions may represent the only portion of the mammalian genome that effectively regulates transcription.
source: Rather, chromatin-accessible regions may represent the only portion of the mammalian genome that effectively regulates transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the findings.

claim: Chromatin-accessible regions in mammals are conserved at levels similar to those in birds and insects.
source: As a result, chromatin-accessible regions in mammals are conserved at levels similar to those in birds and insects, in contrast to the genome as a whole.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The regulatory potential of repetitive and other rapidly-evolving elements could be rendered functionally inconsequential by silencing.
source: The regulatory potential of repetitive and other rapidly-evolving elements could be rendered functionally inconsequential by silencing, or could be concentrated on controlling the expression of genetic elements that we did not investigate, such as non-coding RNAs or species-specific genes (Sundaram et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings, with citation support for the possibility.

claim: Transcriptional networks in birds and insects could diverge under the action of natural selection through specific single nucleotide substitutions resulting in rapid compensatory turnover.
source: In these organisms, transcriptional networks would diverge under the action of natural selection, through specific single nucleotide substitutions resulting in rapid compensatory turnover (He et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is an alternative speculative model proposed to explain the findings, with citation support.

claim: In mammals, transcriptional networks could diverge in a largely neutral fashion driven for instance by transposable elements.
source: In mammals, transcriptional networks would diverge in a largely neutral fashion driven for instance by transposable elements (Sundaram et al., 2014).
evidence: This is part of an alternative speculative model, with citation support.

claim: Similar rates of transcriptional divergence across lineages could arise through very different evolutionary processes.
source: In this case, similar rates of transcriptional divergence across lineages would arise through very different evolutionary processes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how the observed patterns could arise.

claim: None of the proposed models account for the differences in generation times between lineages.
source: Importantly, none of the aforementioned models account for the differences in generation times between lineages.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the proposed explanatory models.

claim: Evolutionary changes occurring based on chronological time and not generation time has also been observed for many protein-coding sequences.
source: Evolutionary changes occurring based on chronological time and not generation time has also been observed for many protein-coding sequences.
evidence: This is a statement about known patterns in molecular evolution.

claim: Observations of chronological evolutionary clocks led to the molecular clock theory.
source: Observations such as these led to the molecular clock theory (Kumar, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: The mechanisms through which environmental forces entrain chronological evolutionary clocks remain to be elucidated.
source: The mechanisms through which environmental forces entrain these chronological evolutionary clocks remain to be elucidated (Kumar, 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in evolutionary biology, supported by citation.
